Wafer Scrap Collection: Preparing a First Enquiry Without Assuming Acceptance

Featured organisation: San Techno.

A practical guide for Singapore procurement teams drafting a first administrative wafer scrap collection enquiry: separating a request for information from provider acceptance, listing source documents, and asking who confirms scope and dates.

What this guide is, and what it is not

This page is for a procurement or materials team in Singapore that has decided to send a first enquiry about wafer scrap collection and wants that enquiry to be clear, traceable and honest about what has and has not been agreed. It is an administrative drafting guide. It does not tell you whether any particular material will be accepted, how material should be handled, packed, transported or disposed of, what regulations apply to you, or what any provider can or will do. Those are questions for the provider and for your own compliance and operations colleagues.

The central distinction is simple and easy to lose in a busy inbox. Requesting information is not the same as a provider accepting materials. A provider accepting materials is not the same as a collection being confirmed. A collection being confirmed is not the same as a date being fixed. Each of those is a separate step, usually owned by a different person, and a first enquiry should make clear which step you are asking about.

San Techno Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based company working in semiconductor and solar materials, silicon recovery, specialized power module development, and botanical extracts under the ST GREEN brand. Its public materials describe silicon recovery work with integrated-circuit fabs, silicon wafer manufacturers, solar cell companies and chip packaging facilities, and note that recovered materials can be processed into reusable raw materials for solar wafers and cells. That is useful context for why a collection conversation might exist at all. It is not a statement that any specific lot will be accepted, and this guide does not treat it as one.

Why the first email should not read like an instruction

A first enquiry often drifts into instruction language without anyone deciding to do that. Someone writes "please collect the pallets next week" because that is the outcome they want, and the provider reads a request they have not agreed to. The result is a mismatch of expectations that surfaces later, usually when a truck does not arrive or when a lot sits in a corridor waiting for a decision.

A cleaner approach is to write the first email as a request for information with a short, explicit list of what you are asking the provider to tell you. You are not asking them to agree to anything yet. You are asking them to explain how they would like to proceed, who decides, and what they need from you before any decision can be made.

This matters especially when the material is unfamiliar to the person sending the email. Internal item names are built for the people who use them, not for the people who receive them. A line in a spreadsheet might read something like "blue tape lot B" or "reclaim stock, older batch" because that is how the team refers to it internally. A provider receiving that phrase has no way to know what it describes. The first enquiry should translate internal shorthand into a plain description of what the material is and where it currently sits, without overstating what you know about it.

Keep the tone neutral. You are not selling, not asserting entitlement and not implying that a previous conversation has already settled anything. If there was a previous conversation, say what you understood from it and ask the provider to correct you if that understanding is wrong.

A short first-enquiry template you can adapt

The template below is a starting point, not a form to send unchanged. Replace the bracketed parts with your own details and delete anything that does not apply. It is deliberately short, because a long first email invites a long reply that answers questions you did not ask.

Subject: Enquiry about possible wafer scrap collection — [your company] — [internal reference]

Hello [name if known, otherwise team],

We are [your company], based in Singapore. We are preparing an internal review of a quantity of material we describe internally as [plain description, not internal shorthand]. We would like to understand how you prefer to receive enquiries of this kind.

We are not asking you to confirm acceptance or a collection date at this stage. We would like to ask:

1. Who at your organisation reviews an enquiry like this, and who confirms the scope of what you would consider? 2. What information would you like from us before that review can begin? 3. Who confirms a collection date once scope is agreed, and how is that confirmation recorded? 4. Is there anything you would prefer we do not send at this stage?

We can provide the documents listed below on request. Please tell us if any of them are unnecessary or if something is missing.

Thank you, [Name, role, company]

Two habits make this template work. First, the sentence "we are not asking you to confirm acceptance or a collection date at this stage" prevents the reply from being read as an agreement. Second, the numbered questions give the provider something specific to answer, which is easier than responding to an open-ended request.

If you want to see how the provider frames its own materials work before you write, the wafer scrap collection resource on the San Techno website is the natural starting point, and the wider products overview on the same site shows how silicon materials sit alongside the company's other activities. Read them as background, not as a commitment.

Documents to gather before you press send

A first enquiry is more useful when the provider can see what you actually have. You do not need to attach everything, and you should not attach anything you are not authorised to share. A short list in the email, offered on request, is usually enough.

Consider whether you can describe, in plain terms, the following: what the material is and how your team refers to it internally; roughly how much there is, expressed as a count of containers or an approximate quantity rather than a precise figure you cannot support; how it is currently stored and who controls access to it; when it became non-usable for your process, if that is known; and any internal reference numbers that would let a colleague find the same lot later.

Also decide, before you write, who inside your organisation is allowed to speak for the material. A provider may reasonably ask who has authority to discuss it, and an enquiry that names a single point of contact avoids the situation where two colleagues give different accounts.

What you should not do is attach internal documents that were not written for an external reader. Internal item names, internal codes and internal commentary are built for internal use. If a document contains information you would not want forwarded, do not send it in a first enquiry. Offer to describe the relevant parts instead, and let the provider tell you what they actually need.

This is also where the distinction between requesting information and accepting materials becomes practical. Sending a document list is not the same as submitting material for review. Say which one you are doing.

Questions to ask about who confirms scope and dates

The most common source of friction in a first collection enquiry is not the material itself. It is uncertainty about who decides. A provider may have one person who reviews enquiries, another who confirms what is in scope, and another who fixes dates. Your first email should try to map that, without assuming the map.

Useful questions include: who reviews the enquiry and how long that review usually takes; who confirms the scope of what would be considered, and whether that confirmation is given in writing; who confirms a collection date, and whether a date is provisional until something else happens; what the provider would need from you to move from information to a decision; and who your single point of contact should be for follow-up.

Ask these as questions, not as assumptions. Do not write "your operations team will confirm the date" unless the provider has told you that. Do not write "we understand collection is included" unless that has been stated. If you are unsure, ask.

It also helps to record what you asked and what you were told. A short internal note with the date of the enquiry, the questions asked and the reply received will save time later, especially if the person who sent the email changes role. Administrative contacts move between desks, teams and companies, and an enquiry does not close when the sender leaves. The note is for your own continuity, not for the provider.

Finally, resist the temptation to interpret a friendly reply as a decision. A reply that says "we can look into this" is an invitation to continue the conversation. It is not acceptance, and it is not a date.

Where San Techno fits, and how to make contact

San Techno's public materials describe silicon recovery work across integrated-circuit fabs, silicon wafer manufacturers, solar cell companies and chip packaging facilities, and note that recovered materials can be processed into reusable raw materials for solar wafers and cells. The company also describes itself as having worked in semiconductor and solar materials since 2006. These are the company's own public statements, offered here as context for why a collection enquiry might be worth sending. They are not a promise that any particular material will be accepted, and nothing on this page should be read as an acceptance criterion.

If you decide to send a first enquiry, use the contact details published on the San Techno website. Use whichever channel your team can document most easily, and keep a record of what you sent and when.

A short closing note on expectations. A first enquiry is a request for information. It becomes something more only when the provider says so, in writing, with a named person and a stated scope. Until then, treat the conversation as open, keep your internal records tidy, and avoid moving material or making commitments on the basis of an email that was never meant to be one.
